situation (example wording): "Shoplifting in Kansas City in 2024", "... in Baltimore", "... in Washington" (a place name that fits more than one place)
what the app does today: Each path picks one reading: the reader fills in a state it was not given ("Columbus" -> Ohio), or declines the name as ambiguous.
proposed behavior: A city named without a state: when two or more states have a city of that name with at least 100,000 people, ask which, with a button for each; otherwise use the most populous, without asking. The same rule when the name fits agencies of different kinds: a city and a county (Baltimore city or Baltimore County), with the same 100,000 floor for the county's agency. A name that is also a state ("Washington") always offers the state beside its large cities and counties. A state named in the question narrows the choice to that state. A city name means the city's principal police agency, named in the answer (a combined city-county agency such as Las Vegas included). A county name means the county police department where one polices the county (Montgomery County, Maryland; Fairfax County, Virginia), otherwise the sheriff's agency, named in the answer (rule 10). The wording settles the ask when it names one reading: "city of X", "X city" or "X Police Department" is the city's principal agency, "NYPD" or "New York City" is the city, "New York State" or a statewide measure is the state; a county named by itself stays the county. A name that fits both the city and the state ("New York" alone) is asked about, with two buttons.
exact default or choices offered: Buttons, one per real candidate, most likely first: e.g. Kansas City, Missouri; Kansas City, Kansas. Baltimore city, Maryland; Baltimore County, Maryland. Washington, D.C.; Washington state; Washington County, Oregon; Washington County, Maryland. New York City (NYPD); New York State.
why: A city in another state, or a county beside its city, is a different place with a different count; asking costs one click.
status: Decided 2026-10-29 (Jeff: "Yes, 100%, same issue with a city/county that share a name (Baltimore, Washington, etc)")
